headline: Connecticut public college system faces leadership reset as accountability debate widens
dek: A succession of departures and investigations has left CSCU relying on interim leaders while state officials debate whether the problem is individual conduct, the system's structure, or both.
body: Connecticut's public college system is entering a new phase of leadership uncertainty after a series of high-level departures, investigations and governance disputes. A [CT Insider report](https://www.ctinsider.com/news/education/article/cscu-leadership-accountability-lamont-fazio-22455854.php) published Oct. 6 said the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system is navigating vacancies and several interim leaders while officials argue over who is responsible for restoring public confidence.

The stakes are statewide. CSCU serves about 100,000 students through Connecticut's four state universities, Connecticut State Community College and its 12 campuses, and Charter Oak State College, according to CT Insider and a [Connecticut Mirror overview](https://ctmirror.org/2026/05/26/natalie-braswell-named-interim-chancellor-of-cscu-system/). Leadership disruption at the system office therefore reaches far beyond one campus: it affects the institutions that educate workers, train nurses and teachers, and provide lower-cost transfer routes for students across the state.

The recent sequence began with the departure of former Chancellor Terrence Cheng after state scrutiny of spending and expense practices, followed in April by the resignation of interim Chancellor O. John Maduko while he was under investigation over allegations of sexual harassment and inappropriate workplace conduct. CT Mirror reported on both the resignation and the system's decision to place General Counsel Karen Buffkin on paid leave amid questions about how the complaint was handled. Those allegations were not criminal findings, and the personnel actions did not by themselves establish every claim made about the officials.

The turmoil deepened in September. An independent review by Grand River Solutions found serious failures in the system's handling of the Maduko matter and faulted multiple officials, according to the current CT Insider report. On Sept. 23, Central Connecticut State University President Zulma Toro announced her resignation after administrators raised allegations of bullying and intimidation. [CT Mirror reported](https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/23/ccsu-zulma-toro-resigns-bullying-allegations/) that CSCU said the concerns were serious but that its investigation into Toro would not continue after her resignation and retirement; the report did not establish that the allegations were proven.

That same day, Board of Regents Vice Chair Juanita James resigned, citing what she described as a dysfunctional culture and political infighting, CT Insider reported. The departures have produced an argument that is partly about personnel and partly about design. Connecticut created the consolidated system in 2011 by bringing its community colleges, regional state universities and online college under a Board of Regents and central office. Supporters have said a statewide structure can make transfers and shared services easier; critics question whether concentrating authority at the top makes it harder to detect problems and assign responsibility.

Former CSCU President Mark Ojakian offered the counterargument in a [Connecticut Public interview](https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-06-17/major-leader-of-ct-higher-ed-consolidation-effort-breaks-silence-to-defend-cscu-system), saying the recent scandals reflected individual leadership failures rather than proof that consolidation itself was broken. Faculty and other critics have pointed to repeated executive turnover and long-running funding pressure as evidence that the structure also deserves review. Those are competing interpretations, not settled findings, and the distinction matters as officials consider changes that could affect every public college in the state.

Interim Chancellor Natalie Braswell has said the system will announce reforms involving compliance, leadership vetting and governance in the coming weeks. CT Insider reported that the Board of Regents has 15 voting seats, with appointments divided among the governor, legislative leaders and students, and that five seats were vacant at the time of the report. The arrangement gives several institutions a role in oversight, but it can also blur the answer to a basic public question: who must act when a concern crosses from a campus office into system leadership?

The immediate next steps are the search for a permanent chancellor, decisions about interim leadership at affected institutions and the promised governance proposals. Legislative leaders have indicated that CSCU-related legislation is likely when the General Assembly returns in January. For students and employees, the practical test will be whether those steps produce clearer reporting channels, credible investigations and stable leadership without interrupting campus services. The system has acknowledged the need for accountability; the coming months will show whether that promise becomes a durable change in how Connecticut's public colleges are run.
location: Connecticut State Colleges and Universities, statewide
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut CSCU leadership turmoil and accountability debate
seoDescription: Connecticut's public college system faces interim leadership, investigations and a governance debate after a succession of high-level departures.
